title: Toeplitz Block Mixing for Scalable Multi-Head Linear Attention

raw.stage1:
### Purpose:
The contribution's purpose is to show that the full \( M \times M \) block mixing matrix in Multi-Head Linear Attention (MHLA) is over-parameterized. Paper [6] discusses redundancy and over-parameterization in Multi-Head Attention (MHA), specifically noting that attention heads often learn similar features and can be pruned without harming performance. Paper [10] also addresses over-parameterization in MHA, observing that trained attention heads share common key/query projections and proposing collaborative mechanisms to reduce redundancy. Both papers establish the same problem-class level objective: identifying and addressing over-parameterization in multi-head attention mechanisms. Thus, the purpose is covered.

### Mechanism:
The contribution fits the learned MHLA mixing matrices to a distance-tied (translation-invariant) kernel to show that coefficients depend primarily on relative block distance. Paper [7] investigates translation-invariant kernels for multivariable approximation, discussing their properties and suitability for function approximation tasks. Paper [8] applies translation-invariant kernel functions in constructing \(\mathcal{H}^2\)-matrices, leveraging the property to reduce computational complexity. Paper [12] explores translational equivariance in kernelizable attention, emphasizing relative interactions between elements. These papers collectively cover the mechanism, as they all utilize translation-invariant kernels to analyze or approximate relationships tied to relative distances.

### Evaluation:
The contribution uses a distance-tied kernel fit yielding \( R^2 > 0.995 \) across all layers. Paper [7] evaluates translation-invariant kernels for function approximation tasks, using metrics like convergence rates and approximation accuracy. Paper [8] validates the efficiency of \(\mathcal{H}^2\)-matrices constructed with translation-invariant kernels, demonstrating computational advantages. Paper [12] evaluates translational equivariance in kernelizable attention using metrics tied to relative positional accuracy. These prior works employ similar evaluation designs (kernel fit accuracy and metrics tied to translation invariance), even though the specific benchmark instance differs. Thus, the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain:
The contribution operates in the domain of efficient attention/sequence modeling. Paper [4] addresses efficient attention computation, focusing on reducing quadratic complexity in transformers for applications like web-page translation and query-answering. Paper [5] targets sparse attention methods to accelerate long-context inference in LLMs. Paper [13] explores sparse and low-rank attention approximations for efficient transformers. These papers all work within the general application area of efficient attention/sequence modeling, even if the specific sub-problems differ. Thus, the domain is covered.

**PURPOSE: Shows that the full M×M block mixing matrix in Multi-Head Linear Attention (MHLA) is over-parameterized.**

The purpose is to demonstrate over-parameterization in a specific attention mechanism (MHLA) by showing that the mixing matrix has redundant degrees of freedom. Papers [6], [10], [22] discuss over-parameterization/redundancy in multi-head attention. Paper [10] explicitly states "they suffer from over-parameterization" and paper [6] mentions "redundancy and over-parameterization" in MHA. However, these papers address over-parameterization in standard (softmax) multi-head attention heads/projections, not in the block mixing matrix of Multi-Head *Linear* Attention specifically. The specific claim — that the M×M block mixing matrix is over-parameterized because coefficients depend only on relative block distance — is a different empirical relationship than head pruning or shared projections. None of the prior papers establish this specific relationship (translation-invariance of block mixing weights in MHLA). NONE.

**MECHANISM: Fits learned MHLA mixing matrices to a distance-tied (translation-invariant) kernel to show coefficients depend primarily on relative block distance.**

This involves fitting learned weight matrices to a translation-invariant (Toeplitz-like) kernel structure as an analysis tool. Paper [12] discusses "Translational Equivariance in Kernelizable Attention" and explicitly studies translation-invariant structure in attention kernels. Paper [25] discusses block-Toeplitz matrices in the context of masked Transformers. Paper [33] discusses estimation and selection of Toeplitz covariance structure. However, none of these papers use the specific mechanism of *fitting* learned attention mixing matrices post-hoc to a distance-tied kernel to diagnose over-parameterization. The closest is [25] which uses block-Toeplitz structure analytically, not as a fitting/diagnostic tool. NONE.

**EVALUATION: Distance-tied kernel fit yields R² > 0.995 across all layers.**

The evaluation design is: fit a structured model to learned weight matrices, report R² goodness-of-fit across layers. This is a regression/curve-fitting evaluation with R² as the metric. This is a standard statistical evaluation design (R² from regression fitting). Paper [33] uses entropy loss for covariance structure fitting. No prior paper uses this exact design (fitting attention mixing matrices to a translation-invariant kernel and reporting R²), but R² as a goodness-of-fit metric in a regression/fitting context is entirely standard. However, the specific protocol — fitting learned neural network weight matrices to a structured kernel and reporting R² per layer — does not appear as a named benchmark or protocol in any prior paper. This is a newly constructed evaluation protocol for this specific diagnostic purpose. NONE.

**DOMAIN: Efficient attention / sequence modeling.**

Multiple prior papers operate in efficient attention and sequence modeling: [4] (efficient attention computation), [5] (sparse attention for long-context LLMs), [13] (sparse and low-rank attention), [16] (linear self-attention), [25] (scalable masked Transformers), [26] (linear transformers). This domain is clearly covered. Paper [4] is representative.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to remove the \(O(M^2)\) block-mixing bottleneck of MHLA and enable extrapolation to longer sequences. Papers [6], [9], [11], [16], [24], and [25] all address length extrapolation in Transformers, which is the same problem-class objective. For example, [6] proposes kernelized relative positional embeddings for extrapolation, [9] introduces position representation methods for extrapolation, and [25] explicitly focuses on improving attention resolution for length extrapolation. These papers share the same purpose of enabling efficient extrapolation to longer sequences, even though the specific mechanisms differ.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, Toeplitz Block Mixing (TBM), parameterizes the mixing kernel as a mixture of exponentials \(K(\delta) = \sum_r a_r \exp(-\lambda_r \delta)\), constraining mixing to depend only on block distance. Papers [12], [26], and [18] describe substantively equivalent mechanisms. For example, [12] approximates power-law kernels using a sum of exponentials, [26] develops a sum-of-exponentials method for kernel functions, and [18] studies exponential kernels in machine learning. These works share the same underlying primitive of using exponential parameterizations for kernel functions, even if applied in different contexts.

### Evaluation
The evaluation reduces mixing complexity from \(O(M^2 d^2)\) to \(O(M R d^2)\) for kernel rank \(R \ll M\) and supports length extrapolation since the kernel is defined for any distance. Papers [6], [9], [11], [16], [24], and [25] use similar evaluation designs for validating extrapolation capabilities in Transformers. For example, [6] evaluates kernelized relative positional embeddings for extrapolation, [9] tests position representation methods for extrapolation, and [25] measures attention resolution improvements for length extrapolation. These papers share the same evaluation design of validating extrapolation performance, even if applied to different benchmarks or datasets.

### Domain
The domain is linear attention architectures. Papers [1], [2], [6], [9], [11], [16], and [25] all work within the general application area of linear attention architectures. For example, [1] studies scalability in self-attention mechanisms, [2] focuses on hardware-efficient linear attention, and [6] addresses kernelized relative positional embeddings in linear attention. These papers share the same domain of linear attention architectures, even if targeting different sub-problems or datasets.
